opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the basic intuition is surprisingly simple. When you generate synthetic math problems at scale, you can't afford to have humans check every one. Even if you could, verifying solutions to harder problems is expensive and error-prone for people too. So the question becomes: can the model's own behavior tell you something about whether a problem and its answer are trustworthy?

What we lean on is self-consistency. For a given synthetic problem, you sample many independent solution attempts, ideally with some diversity in temperature, prompting, or even different models, and then you look at how the final answers distribute. If a strong majority of those reasoning paths converge on the same answer, that's a pretty good signal that the problem is well-posed and the answer is likely correct. If the answers are scattered all over the place, that tells you something is off. Maybe the problem is ambiguous, underspecified, or just broken, or it's beyond what the model can reliably solve.

So agreement becomes a proxy for quality, and you use it as a filter. You keep the high-agreement examples and discard or down-weight the rest.

That said, I want to be careful, because consistency isn't the same as correctness. Models can be confidently, consistently wrong. If a model has a systematic misconception, all the samples might march off the same cliff together. So there are a few things we think about to make this more robust.

One is diversity of the solvers. If different models, or the same model with very different solution strategies, like algebraic reasoning versus writing code to compute the answer, still agree, that's much stronger evidence than one model agreeing with itself.

Another is the threshold. You don't want just a plurality. You want a high level of agreement, and you can tune that threshold as a tradeoff between data quantity and data quality.

And third, you have to watch what the filter does to your distribution. If you only keep problems everyone finds easy to agree on, you can end up biased toward easier problems and lose the hard, interesting ones that actually push the model forward. So part of the craft is balancing agreement-based filtering with keeping enough difficulty in the mix.

But overall, what's exciting is that this kind of answer consistency works far better than you might expect as a substitute for human validation. It lets smaller models, or open efforts without huge annotation budgets, build high-quality math training data. And that connects to a broader theme I care about: we don't necessarily need brute-force scale and massive human labeling if we're clever about how we generate, verify, and curate data.

r001.rationale: The response says to sample multiple independent solutions to the same synthetic math problem and use convergence on the same final answer as a signal of quality.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something we spent a lot of time on, because the whole premise of the work was: can you generate large amounts of math data synthetically, from a model, without having humans go in and check every problem? And the obvious failure mode is that the model generates a problem and then produces a wrong answer, and now you're training on garbage.

So the idea with answer consistency is pretty simple. For each synthetic problem, instead of trusting a single solution, you sample multiple solutions, say ten or twenty, and you look at whether they converge on the same final answer. If the model solves a problem ten different ways and gets the same number every time, that's a reasonably strong signal that the answer is right, or at least that the problem is well-posed and the answer is stable. If the answers are all over the place, that tells you something is off, either the problem is ambiguous, or it's beyond what the model can reliably do, and in both cases you probably don't want it in your training set.

Now, I want to be honest that this is a proxy, not ground truth. Consistency is not correctness. A model can be confidently and consistently wrong, especially on problems that hit a systematic blind spot. So we did try to calibrate this. We took a subset where we did have verified answers, and we looked at how well majority-vote agreement predicted actual correctness. And what you find is that when agreement is very high, correctness is also quite high, but it's not perfect, and the relationship degrades as you go to harder problems. So you end up with a threshold that's really a tradeoff: filter aggressively and you keep mostly correct data but you also bias toward easier problems, because those are the ones the model agrees on. Filter loosely and you get more diversity and difficulty but more noise.

And that difficulty bias is the thing I'd flag as the real concern. If you only keep problems where the model is already consistent, you're kind of teaching it what it already knows. So we experimented with a few things around that, like using a stronger model to generate solutions than the one you're going to train, or treating the lower-agreement problems differently rather than throwing them out entirely, say by keeping the problem but not the answer. The other thing that helps is combining consistency with cheap structural checks, whether the answer is in the right form, whether the solution actually references the quantities in the problem, that kind of thing. None of those alone is enough, but together they get you surprisingly far.

So my overall take is: answer consistency is a very useful, very cheap filter, and in practice it removes a large fraction of the junk. But I'd be careful about treating it as validation. It's more like a difficulty-weighted confidence score, and you should design your pipeline knowing that's what it is.

r001.rationale: It describes sampling multiple solutions to the same synthetic math problem and using agreement on their final answers as a proxy for answer reliability and data quality.

astra-6.text:
I think answer consistency is a useful signal, but we have to be careful about what it tells us. If you solve the same math problem several different ways and arrive at the same answer, that gives you more confidence. You can use that agreement to filter synthetic examples without having a human check every one.

But consistency is not the same as correctness. A model can make the same mistake repeatedly, especially if the solutions share the same underlying assumptions. So agreement among genuinely different approaches is more informative than agreement among slightly different versions of the same reasoning.

There’s also a selection effect: if we keep only problems where the model consistently agrees with itself, we may end up keeping mostly easy problems. So I would treat consistency as a scalable quality filter, while recognizing that it neither guarantees correctness nor tells us whether the resulting data has the diversity and difficulty we need.

r001.rationale: It says that solving the same math problem several ways and arriving at the same answer increases confidence, and that this agreement can filter synthetic examples.

sol-6.1.text:
I think consistency is a useful signal, but it’s not the same as correctness. A model can produce the same wrong answer repeatedly, especially if there’s a systematic mistake in how it approaches a problem. So if we generate several solutions and they agree, that gives us some confidence, but it doesn’t replace validation.

For math, we can sometimes do better by checking the answer computationally or verifying intermediate steps. We can also look for agreement across different approaches, rather than just sampling the same model repeatedly. But those checks have their own limits. I would use answer consistency as one filter for synthetic data quality, while being careful about treating that agreement as ground truth.

r001.rationale: It says that generating several solutions to a math problem and seeing them agree provides confidence and can serve as a filter for synthetic data quality.
